corrections.compiler_and_flags: Quoted C/C++ rows are 'prod' builds (make -j prod). corrections.caveats: This compares libraries and parsers, not languages. The README says library-based tests (JSON, Base64, CSV) use 'the best practical option for each language'. Rust (rust/src/benchmarks/csv_parse.rs) uses the simd-csv 0.13 crate (a pure-Rust SIMD CSV reader, MIT) and str::parse::<f64>. Zig (zig/src/csv_parse.zig) uses the csvzero package and std.fmt.parseFloat. C (c/src/csv.c) is a hand-written byte-at-a-time state machine for quotes and commas that copies each numeric field into a 64-byte stack buffer and calls glibc strtod. C++ (cpp/src/csv_parse.cpp) uses the lazycsv header library and std::stod on a temporary std::string per field. The workload is 3 floats per row, 100,000 rows and 70 iterations (run.js). The prod C/C++ builds use -O2 with hardening while Rust uses opt-level 3, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe C/C++ rows are just as slow, so optimisation level does not explain the gap. The suite benchmarked no C or C++ build with a fast float parser (fast_float, std::from_chars) or a SIMD CSV library. Single machine, one monthly run, run by the suite author, who calls the suite subjective.
corrections.why_faster: The suite states no mechanism; this is from reading the sources. The difference is the choice of library and float parser. Rust splits fields with the simd-csv crate's SIMD reader and parses them with core's Eisel-Lemire-based f64 parser. C uses a scalar byte loop plus glibc strtod on a copied field, and C++ uses lazycsv plus std::stod on a temporary string. Zig also uses a CSV package with std.fmt.parseFloat and reaches 0.974 s, which fits the parser being the dominant factor. No profile separates field splitting from float parsing.

notes: The numbers match the CSV::Parse-runtime entries of results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js. Metadata checks out: MIT, 41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08. D is arguable under the crippled-baseline precedent (naive C loop against a tuned crate); it is held at C because the C++ side also uses a CSV library and the C build is a normal release build. baseline_stdlib is left empty: no -stdlib flag is set, so clang++ presumably used libstdc++, but this was not checked.

Neither side uses -march; the suite rules forbid hardware targeting. Rust: cargo build --release with the rust/Cargo.toml release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" (default opt-level 3), plus hashbrown 0.14.3, aligned-vec 0.5 and serde_json. Compiler versions are not stated: the Docker image is archlinux:base with an unpinned pacman clang and rustup stable (dockerfiles/base.Dockerfile, dockerfiles/rust.Dockerfile).

corrections.caveats: The suite gives no mechanism. The timed region ('Processing time (w/o IO)') excludes JSON parsing and writing on both sides, so nlohmann/json versus serde_json does not affect the table. It does dominate whole-process time: C++ 3.35 s versus Rust 1.27 s at 60k posts, with 460 MB versus 29 MB RSS. Inside the timed region both programs run the same algorithm: per-tag lists of post indices, uint8 shared-tag counters, a scan in 64-entry chunks with a running minimum, and 5-slot top-k insertion. The tuning differs. Rust zeroes each 64-byte chunk right after scanning it, on a 64-byte-aligned counter buffer padded to a multiple of 64. C++ memsets the whole counter array before each post and uses bounds-checked std::vector::at() for every counter access in the hot loops. The tag index is hashbrown in Rust and std::unordered_map<std::string, unique_ptr<vector<int>>> in C++; Rust re-hashes each tag string per post, while C++ caches per-post pointers. The suite has no C solution. The solutions are community-written and were run on a cloud VM (10 runs at 5k posts, 3 at 20k and 60k) with compiler versions and CPU model unstated. Zig (1.93 s) and Odin (2.00 s) are slower than C++. The Rust HO row (51.55 ms) uses specialised data structures and is excluded. The repository now lives at zupat/related_post_gen, and the jinyus URL redirects there.
corrections.why_faster: The suite states none. From the sources, the timed loops use the same algorithm and the differences are implementation tuning. Rust folds the counter reset into the chunk scan on an aligned, padded buffer; C++ makes a separate memset pass per post and uses bounds-checked .at() accesses. Nobody measured which of these explains the 1.26-1.28x gap. The win is not shown to be a language property, and the C++ multicore version beats Rust's.

tier_reason: The harness is A-grade: json/json.rs/src/json_pull.rs and json_struct.rs against json/test_yyjson.c and test_gason.cpp, flags in common/commands.mk and json/Makefile, gcc 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8, Rust 1.97.1 and a Xeon E-2324G. But it compares a streaming typed deserializer with DOM parsers (same_algorithm false), the C yyjson baseline is a distro-built shared library, and C++ parsers doing comparable work beat Rust. Capped at C (unequal-work precedent).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Json table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README update 2026-07-19): Rust (Serde Custom) 0.103 s and Rust (Serde Typed) 0.110 s versus C/gcc (yyjson) 0.131 s, C/clang (yyjson) 0.132 s, C++/g++ (gason) 0.127 s, C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154 s (clang++ 0.194 s) and C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374 s. Serde Custom is about 1.27x faster than gcc yyjson and 1.23x faster than g++ gason (derived from page data). It is not faster than C++/g++ simdjson On-Demand 0.060 s, C++/clang++ DAW JSON Link 0.085 s (NoCheck 0.070 s), or C++/clang++ simdjson DOM 0.103 s (a tie; g++ 0.107 s). Rust doing like-for-like DOM parsing (Serde Untyped, serde_json::Value) takes 0.557 s, about 4.3x slower than C yyjson (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries and -std=c23 or -std=c++23; clang++ adds -stdlib=libc++ (common/commands.mk). gason, RapidJSON, simdjson and DAW JSON Link are compiled from source with these flags. The C yyjson rows instead link Debian's libyyjson-dev shared library (json/Makefile: $(GCC_BUILD) -lyyjson; docker/Dockerfile installs libyyjson-dev), so the yyjson parser was built with the distro's packaging flags, not -O3 -march=native -flto. Rust 1.97.1: RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C llvm-args=--x86-branches-within-32B-boundaries' cargo build --release, with the json/json.rs/Cargo.toml profile lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort; serde_json 1.0.150 and serde 1.0.228.
corrections.caveats: This compares libraries and algorithms, not languages. Rust (Serde Custom), in json/json.rs/src/json_pull.rs, is a serde-derived typed deserializer. Its visitor folds the x, y and z sums while streaming and skips the name and opts fields without building them (memory increase 0.00 MiB). Rust (Serde Typed), in json_struct.rs, collects a Vec<Coordinate> (+11.12 MiB). The C and C++ baselines named in the record are DOM parsers that materialise the whole document: yyjson +229.38 MiB, gason +96.75 MiB, RapidJSON +123.44 MiB. C++ schema-driven or on-demand parsers doing comparable work are faster (simdjson On-Demand 0.060 s, DAW JSON Link 0.085 s), and Rust doing DOM work (Serde Untyped) takes 0.557 s. The C yyjson rows use the distro-built shared library rather than a build with the suite's -O3 -march=native -flto. The README notes number-parsing inaccuracies in gason, default RapidJSON and DAW JSON Link, and that gason mutates its input and simdjson needs padded input. The input is 524,288 generated coordinate objects (json/generate_json.rb). File reading is outside the timed region on both sides.
corrections.why_faster: The README states none; this is from the sources. The two sides use different parsing strategies. serde's derive generates a schema-specific deserializer, so Rust (Serde Custom) parses only the three numeric fields into a running sum and skips the rest without allocating. The C/C++ baselines build a full DOM of all 524,288 objects before computing the sums. When C++ takes a comparable schema-driven or on-demand approach (simdjson On-Demand, DAW JSON Link) it beats Rust, and Rust building a DOM (Serde Untyped) is about 4x slower than yyjson. So the win comes from the API and algorithm, not the language.

notes: The numbers match the README Json table row for row. Shortcoming: the win is a typed streaming deserializer against DOM parsers. C++ simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s) and DAW JSON Link (0.085 s) beat it, and Rust's own DOM row (0.557 s) is 4.3x slower than yyjson, so this is not a Rust language advantage.
